lead: Any linear network with two output terminals, however many resistors and sources sit inside it, behaves at those terminals like one voltage source in series with one resistor. Thevenin's theorem names that source V_th and that resistor R_th; Norton's theorem describes the same network as one current source I_N in parallel with R_N. The two forms are one circuit seen from outside. Engineers use them to replace a messy supply or bias network by two numbers, so load current and load voltage follow from a single loop.
prereq: You need: 2.1 and 2.2 to solve for the open-circuit voltage and the short-circuit current, plus source transformation from Unit 1.

sections.h3: Thevenin's theorem: open-circuit voltage and dead network

blocks.text: Thevenin's theorem: any linear two-terminal network can be replaced, at its terminals a and b, by one voltage source V_th in series with one resistance R_th. V_th is the open-circuit voltage, the voltage across a-b with the load removed. R_th is the resistance seen looking into a-b with every independent source set to zero.

Those two numbers do all the work. Whatever load you attach, the current it draws depends on the network only through V_th and R_th. A 12 V battery with 0.5 Ω internal resistance, a sensor bridge, the bias network inside an amplifier: each collapses to this pair.

items: Remove the load between a and b and mark the polarity of V_th, for example a positive with respect to b.
Solve the network for the voltage across a-b with the load off. That value is V_th; use nodal or mesh analysis.
Set every independent source to zero: short each ideal voltage source, open each ideal current source. Leave dependent sources as they are.
Look into a-b, combine series and parallel resistances, and that is R_th.
Check by shorting a to b, finding I_sc, and testing R_th = V_th / I_sc.

blocks.text: Setting a source to zero does not delete it. A 0 V voltage source is a perfect wire and a 0 A current source is a gap; the element keeps its place, only its value becomes zero. In circuits with dependent sources R_th can even come out negative. That is a real result, not an arithmetic error.

sections.h3: Norton's form and the swap between the two

blocks.text: Norton's theorem replaces the same network by a current source I_N in parallel with a resistance R_N. I_N is the short-circuit current, the current that flows from a to b through a wire joining the terminals. R_N is found exactly like R_th, with all independent sources dead, and the two resistances are equal: R_N = R_th.

The two forms are linked by source transformation: V_th = I_N R_th and I_N = V_th / R_th. Nodal analysis hands you V_th naturally; mesh analysis hands you I_sc naturally. Choose whichever keeps the arithmetic short.

Fix the sign of I_N as the current leaving terminal a into the external short. Then load current from the voltage form and from the current form agree in direction as well as size. A sign slip in I_N makes the voltage and current forms disagree in direction, and if you compute R_th = V_th/I_sc from a wrongly signed I_sc you will report a negative R_th. A real negative R_th comes only from circuits with dependent sources.

A dependent source has no value of its own; it copies a voltage or current elsewhere in the circuit. It therefore cannot be set to zero when you look for R_th. Only the independent sources die, series-parallel usually cannot finish the job, and you use a test source.

items: Dead every independent source and leave every dependent source in place.
Connect a test voltage source V_t across a-b, positive terminal at a. V_t = 1 V keeps the numbers short; any value works.
Solve the circuit with the dependent source inside the equations and find I_t, the current entering terminal a.
Compute R_th = V_t / I_t. If you injected a test current instead, use the voltage that appears at a-b as V_t.
V_th is still the open-circuit voltage, measured before anything is deaded.

blocks.text: A small setup. Terminals a-b. Inside sits a 3 Ω resistor from a to an internal node c, and a dependent voltage source of value 2V_x whose positive terminal is at c and negative terminal at b, so V_c − V_b = 2V_x (with b as reference, V_c = 2V_x). Here V_x is the voltage across the 3 Ω resistor, so V_x = V_a − V_c. Apply V_t at a with b as reference. The dependent source forces V_c = 2(V_t − V_c), giving V_c = (2/3)V_t and V_x = V_t/3. The test current is I_t = V_x / 3 = V_t / 9, so R_th = V_t / I_t = 9 Ω. No independent source exists, so V_th = 0 and the equivalent is a bare 9 Ω resistor.

figure.caption: A network is reduced at its own two terminals to V_th in series with R_th, using the open-circuit voltage and the resistance of the dead network.

spec.aria: A two-terminal linear network feeds two measurement steps, open-circuit voltage and dead-network resistance, which combine into a V_th plus R_th equivalent at the same terminals.

examples.question: A 12 V independent voltage source is in series with a 4 Ω resistor, and this combination feeds a 6 Ω load connected across the output terminals a-b. Find the Thevenin voltage V_th, the Thevenin resistance R_th, the short-circuit current I_sc and the Norton current I_N of the network seen by the load.
steps: The load is the 6 Ω resistor. Remove it and what remains between a and b is the network: the 12 V source in series with the 4 Ω resistor, with a-b open at the far end of the 4 Ω.
With the load off, no current flows, so there is no drop across the 4 Ω resistor. The open-circuit voltage equals the source voltage: V_th = 12 V, with terminal a positive with respect to b.
Dead the 12 V source: replace it by a short circuit. Looking into a-b, only the 4 Ω resistor remains: R_th = 4 Ω.
For the short-circuit current, join a to b with a wire. The whole 12 V appears across the 4 Ω resistor: I_sc = 12/4 = 3 A.
Check consistency: V_th / R_th = 12/4 = 3 A, which equals I_sc, so the two measurements agree.
The Norton form uses the same resistance and the short-circuit current: I_N = I_sc = 3 A and R_N = R_th = 4 Ω.
examples.answer: V_th = 12 V, R_th = 4 Ω, I_sc = 3 A, I_N = 3 A and R_N = 4 Ω.
examples.check:
Vs = 12.0
R1 = 4.0
Vth = Vs
Rth = R1
Isc = Vs / R1
IN = Vth / Rth
print(Vth)
print(Rth)
print(Isc)
print(IN)

traps: Deading a source the wrong way. A voltage source becomes a short wire; a current source becomes an open gap. Reversing them spoils every later parallel-series step.
Removing a resistor that is part of the network and calling it the load. The load is only the element you deliberately detach; everything else stays.
Forgetting the test source when a dependent source is present, or deading the dependent source too. Its value depends on the circuit, so it must stay in the equations.

Sign of I_N. Fix it as current leaving terminal a into the external short. A sign slip makes the voltage and current forms disagree in direction. Computing R_th = V_th/I_sc from a wrongly signed I_sc gives a false negative R_th; a real negative R_th comes only from dependent sources.
Applying the theorem to a diode or a saturated amplifier. Over a wide range that network is not linear; a Thevenin equivalent then holds only near one operating point.

quiz.q: State Thevenin's theorem and define V_th and R_th.
quiz.a: Any linear two-terminal network equals a voltage source V_th in series with a resistance R_th. V_th is the open-circuit voltage at the terminals; R_th is the resistance seen at the terminals with all independent sources dead.

quiz.q: How is each independent source set to zero when finding R_th?
quiz.a: An ideal voltage source becomes a short circuit (0 V) and an ideal current source becomes an open circuit (0 A). Dependent sources are left in place.

quiz.q: Why does the load current depend on the network only through V_th and R_th?
quiz.a: At the terminals a linear network has a straight-line relation V = V_th − I R_th. Two points, the open-circuit voltage and the short-circuit current, fix that line completely, so every load is just a point on it.

quiz.q: A 10 V source is in series with 5 Ω and feeds a 5 Ω load across the output terminals. Find V_th, R_th and I_N of the network seen by the load.
quiz.a: Remove the 5 Ω load. No current flows, so there is no drop across the series 5 Ω: V_th = 10 V. With the source shorted, R_th = 5 Ω. I_sc = 10/5 = 2 A, and V_th/R_th = 10/5 = 2 A, so I_N = 2 A.

quiz.q: A source has V_th = 9 V and R_th = 3 Ω. Find the current through a 6 Ω load and the terminal voltage.
quiz.a: I = V_th/(R_th + R_L) = 9/(3 + 6) = 1 A. Terminal voltage = 1 × 6 = 6 V.

quiz.q: A network contains a dependent source. Why does series-parallel fail for R_th, and what replaces it?
quiz.a: The dependent source's value follows a voltage or current elsewhere, so it cannot be merged as a fixed resistance. Dead only the independent sources, apply a test source V_t at the terminals, solve for I_t with the dependent source in the equations, then R_th = V_t/I_t.

quiz.q: Two different networks have identical V_th and R_th at their terminals. Are they indistinguishable for every load? Where do they differ?
quiz.a: At the terminals they cannot be told apart: same load current, same terminal voltage, same power delivered. They differ inside, in internal power loss and in the current drawn from the real sources. The equivalence holds only at those two terminals.

beyond: Not for the exam. Circuit simulators such as SPICE build a small-signal Thevenin model around a DC operating point for every transistor, which is how an amplifier's output resistance reaches a datasheet as one number. Battery management chips track open-circuit voltage and internal resistance to estimate state of charge, the same two quantities. Regulator datasheets quote output impedance, which is R_th at the output terminals across a frequency range. Later coursework replaces the two numbers by four, the two-port parameters of Unit 6. Search for 'output impedance of a voltage regulator' or 'Thevenin equivalent of a sensor bridge'.
